rules.title: Common pricing algorithms used in unlawful restraints of trade
rules.requirement: A person, as defined by Section 16702 and excluding an end consumer, must not use or distribute a common pricing algorithm as part of a contract, trust combination, or conspiracy restraining trade or commerce in violation of the Cartwright Act. This prohibition concerns methodologies used by two or more persons that use competitor data to influence a price or commercial term.
rules.exemptions: Section 16729 states no property, ownership, tenancy, or housing-program eligibility conditions. A common pricing algorithm is any methodology, including a computer, software, or other technology, used by two or more persons that uses competitor data to recommend, align, stabilize, set, or otherwise influence a price or commercial term. Distribution includes selling, licensing, providing access, or otherwise making available by any means, including subscriptions or service sales. Commercial terms include service level, availability, and output, including product quantities or the amount or level of service. Price includes money or any other tangible or intangible thing of value expected, required, or given in payment for a product or service, including employee or independent-contractor compensation. Person incorporates Section 16702, whose text is not supplied, and expressly excludes the end consumer of a product or service. These are actor and conduct qualifications, not findings about any address or actual product use.
rules.quoted_span:
16729.
(a) It shall be unlawful for a person to use or distribute a common pricing algorithm as part of a contract, combination in the form of a trust, or conspiracy to restrain trade or commerce in violation of this chapter.
(b) It shall be unlawful for a person to use or distribute a common pricing algorithm if the person coerces another person to set or adopt a recommended price or commercial term recommended by the common pricing algorithm for the same or similar products or services in the jurisdiction of this state.
(c) Nothing in this section shall impair or limit the applicability of antitrust laws.
(d) For purposes of this section, the following definitions apply:
(1) “Antitrust laws” means the provisions of this part.
(2) “Commercial term” includes, without limitation, any of the following:
(A) Level of service.
(B) Availability.
(C) Output, including quantities of products produced or distributed or the amount or level of service provided.
(3) “Common pricing algorithm” means any
methodology, including a computer, software, or other technology, used by two or more persons, that uses competitor data to recommend, align, stabilize, set, or otherwise influence a price or commercial
term.
(4) “Distribute,” “distribution,” and “distributing” include selling, licensing, providing access to, or otherwise making available by any means, including through a subscription or the sale of a service.
(5) “Person” has the same meaning as defined in Section 16702 and does not include the end consumer of a product or service.
(6) “Price” means the amount of money or other thing of value, whether tangible or not, expected, required, or given in payment for any product or service, including compensation paid to an employee or independent contractor for services provided.

rules.title: Prohibition on using defined rent-coordination service providers
rules.requirement: A real estate lessor—an owner leasing real property or a portion of it as a residential dwelling unit—or its agent or subcontractor may not subscribe to, contract with, exchange anything of value for, or otherwise use the services of a service provider as defined in the ordinance.
rules.exemptions: Residential dwelling units must be intended as a person's primary residence and exclude inpatient medical care, licensed long-term care, and detention or correctional facilities. A service provider is a person performing a coordination function, with the source's express cross-reference to Section 1(a)(i)(1), for a real estate lessor or rentor. Person includes a natural person, corporation, partnership, limited liability company, firm, or association. The coordination definition describes collecting nonpublic competitor information from real estate lessors; collecting historical or contemporaneous prices, price changes, supply levels, occupancy rates, or lease or rental contract termination and renewal dates from two or more real estate lessors or public databases; computational analysis or processing of that information; and recommendations using that information concerning rental prices, lease terms, or occupancy levels. Nonpublic competitor information includes prices, supply levels, security deposits, ideal occupancy levels, lease contract termination, renewal dates, or other material lease terms that are less than 365 days old and not widely and readily available to the public at no cost. The coordination definition exempts owners of multiple properties for actions related exclusively to properties controlled by the same rental property owner. Licensed Real Estate Agents operating in accordance with all applicable state regulations are excluded from both the coordination and service-provider definitions. These are qualifications of the regulated actors and services, not findings that any address uses such a service.
rules.citation: Jersey City Code §218-12(2)(1), Ord. 25-076; definitions in §218-12(1), Ord. 25-057
rules.quoted_span:
1.Definitions
a.The following terms, as used in this ordinance, shall have the following meanings:
i.“Coordinate” or “coordinating” mean, with respect to a service provider, collecting nonpublic competitor
information from real estate lessors; and, collecting of historical or contemporaneous prices, price changes, supply
levels, occupancy rates, or lease or rental contract termination and renewal dates of residential dwelling units from
two or more real estate lessors or from public databases;
1.analyzing or processing of the information described in subparagraph (1)(a)(i) using a system, software, or process
that uses computation; and
2.Recommending to any other party rental prices, lease terms, or occupancy levels to a real estate lessorusing the
information described in subparagraph (1)(a)(i).
a.This definition exempts owners of multiple properties for actions related exclusively to multiple properties
controlled by the same rental property owner; and
3.Licensed Real Estate Agents are not included in this definition so long as they are operating in accordance with all
applicable state regulations.
ii.“Person” means any natural person, corporation, partnership, limited liability company, firm, or association.
iii.“Residential dwelling unit” means any house, apartment, accessory unit, or other unit intended to be used as a
person’s primary residence; and does not include inpatient medical care, licensed long-term care, and detention or
correctional facilities.
iv.“Real estate lessor” means any individual, corporation, partnership, association, joint-stock company, trust, or
unincorporated organization that owns real property and leases such property or any portion thereof in the form of a
residential dwelling unit.
v.“Service provider” means any person that performs a coordination function, as defined in Section 1(a)(i)(1) of this
Act, for any real estate lessor or rentor.
1.Licensed Real Estate Agents are not included in this definition so long as they are operating in accordance with all
applicable state regulations.
vi.“Nonpublic Competitor Information” means information, including but not limited to prices, supply levels,
security deposits, ideal occupancy levels, lease contract termination, renewal dates of residential dwelling units or
any other material lease terms that is less than 365 days old and is not widely and readily available to the public at
no cost.
2.Unlawful Conduct
a.It is unlawful for any real estate lessor, agent, or subcontractor thereof, to subscribe to, contract with, or otherwise
exchange anything of value in return for the services of a Service Provider.
b.No service provider shall facilitate an agreement not to compete among real estate lessors with respect to any
aspect of residential dwelling units, including rental pricing, fees, or any other rental terms.
Adopted on second and final reading after hearing on May 21 2025
Date to Mayor: May 22 2025
Approved: May 22 2025

rules.title: Prohibition on algorithmic rent fixing
rules.requirement: Landlords renting covered residential dwelling units in Hoboken must not use software, algorithms, or data-sharing platforms to collect and analyze nonpublic competitor information from other real estate lessors to coordinate, recommend, or implement rental prices, lease terms, or occupancy levels among competing real estate lessors. The Division of Housing or any private citizen alleging to be aggrieved may bring alleged violations to Hoboken Municipal Court; upon conviction, any person violating the chapter is subject to one or more penalties prescribed under N.J.S.A. 40:49-5, a fine not exceeding $2,000, or community service not exceeding 90 days.
rules.coverage_conditions: Covers residential dwelling units in Hoboken used as primary residences, excluding medical/long-term care or detention facilities. The source does not limit its medical exclusion to inpatient care or its long-term-care exclusion to licensed facilities; the available fact vocabulary cannot completely represent these exclusions.
rules.exemptions: Medical/long-term care and detention facilities are excluded from covered residential dwelling units. The prohibition concerns the defined collection and analysis of nonpublic competitor information from other real estate lessors for coordination, recommendation, or implementation among competing lessors, not all pricing tools. Nonpublic competitor information must be less than 365 days old and not widely and readily available to the public at no cost; it includes, without limitation, prices, supply levels, security deposits, ideal occupancy levels, lease contract termination, renewal dates of residential dwelling units, and other material terms.
rules.quoted_span:
A.
Prohibited conduct. Landlords who rent any residential dwelling unit (defined as any primary residence excluding medical/long-term care or detention facilities) in the City of Hoboken are prohibited from price fixing using algorithmic pricing.
For purposes of this chapter, "price fixing using algorithmic pricing" shall be defined as the use of software, algorithms, or data-sharing platforms to collect and analyze nonpublic competitor information from other real estate lessors in order to coordinate, recommend, or implement rental prices, lease terms, or occupancy levels for residential dwelling units among competing real estate lessors.
For purposes of this chapter, "nonpublic competitor information" shall be defined as information including, but not limited to, prices, supply levels, security deposits, ideal occupancy levels, lease contract termination, renewal dates of residential dwelling units or any other material terms that is less than 365 days old and is not widely and readily available to the public at no cost.
B.
Enforcement.
Enforcement. Alleged violations of this chapter may be brought by the Division of Housing, or any private citizen alleging to be aggrieved, to the Hoboken Municipal Court for adjudication.
C.
Penalties. Any person violating the requirements set forth in this chapter shall, upon conviction, be subject to one or more of the following penalties:
Penalties as prescribed under N.J.S.A. 40:49-5; or
By a fine not exceeding $2,000; or
By a period of community service not exceeding 90 days.

review.issue: The January 1, 2026 effective date is derived from the supplied general effective-date guidance and the chaptered 2025 enactment, interpreted as a regular-session, nonurgency statute. It is not an effective date expressly written in AB 325. On this interpretation both prohibitions are in force as of October 1, 2026.
review.quoted_span: A statute enacted during a regular session of the Legislature takes effect on January 1 of the following year, unless a later date is specified in the statute. An urgency statute, which must be approved by a two-thirds majority vote in each house of the Legislature, can take effect immediately after it is signed by the Governor and chaptered into law.

review.issue: Section 16756.1 supplies a complaint pleading standard for Cartwright Act violations, rather than a separate residential address duty.
